Abstract:

Neutron stars (NSs) are natural laboratories for studying dense matter, strong-field gravity, and gravitational-wave phenomena under extreme physical conditions. Their observable properties, such as mass, radius, tidal deformability, and oscillation frequencies, provide important insights into the equation of state (EOS) of dense matter and the nature of gravity. In this seminar, I will talk about the structure, stability, oscillations, and spacetime curvature of neutron stars and proto-neutron stars (PNSs) within the frameworks of General Relativity (GR) and Energy-Momentum Squared Gravity (EMSG). The effects of matter composition, pressure anisotropy, finite temperature, and modified gravity are explored using a variety of hadronic, hybrid, and relativistic mean-field EOSs. Radial and non-radial oscillations are studied to understand stellar stability and constrain fundamental-mode ((f)-mode) frequencies. Universal relations connecting quantities such as compactness, moment of inertia, tidal deformability, and oscillation frequencies are examined and found to remain robust across different EOSs, anisotropy strengths, thermal conditions, and gravity models. The impact of EMSG on neutron-star properties and spacetime curvature is analyzed through mass-radius relations, sound-speed profiles, and curvature scalars. The results provide new constraints on dense matter, reveal possible signatures of phase transitions in stellar interiors, and highlight the potential of multimessenger observations for testing gravity and the physics of compact stars.
